scenarios.title: Shared AI reasoning budgets force organizations to ration expert models, leaving unmonitored tasks to make costly errors
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Mid-sized enterprises and member cooperatives run dozens of specialized software agents for inventory, payroll, tenant intake, and regulatory compliance. Frontier-tier model compute remains scarce and metered. Central corporate IT departments establish internal token budgets or bidding auctions for expert reasoning. A clinic billing agent buys top-tier reasoning to maximize insurer reimbursements, while its medication-reconciliation helper runs on a stripped-down mini-model that silently drops subtle drug-interaction warnings because it lacks the budget to request an expert check.
scenarios.premise: When organizations deploy autonomous software helpers across multiple departments, running the most capable models for every task is too expensive. As a result, teams ration access to expert models by internal price or fiat quotas, which frequently starves quiet but high-stakes compliance or safety tasks while over-serving loud commercial requests.
scenarios.how: The collective intelligence network designs and tests opportunity-cost-aware clearing protocols in simulation and open software that allocate bounded compute based on task criticality and regression risk rather than token plutocracy. By pairing lightweight local models with external deterministic verification gates, member cooperatives are supported in verifying that essential tasks receive expert scrutiny without centralized budget rationing.

outcomes.name: Plutocratic compute rationing starves quiet safety tasks
outcomes.description: High-revenue departments bid up the cost of expert model calls, leaving background safety, privacy audits, and compliance helpers to run on cheap models that make uncorrected mistakes.
outcomes.example: A regional hospital automated patient-discharge assistant runs out of monthly compute budget and approves an incompatible prescription because commercial billing agents consumed 80% of the hospital frontier model quota.

outcomes.name: Opportunity-cost clearing balances collective reasoning
outcomes.description: Member cooperatives and organizations evaluate assistant requests by expected net benefit and task criticality rather than financial bids, establishing minimum verification floors for every critical task.
outcomes.example: A cooperative pharmacy network uses an opportunity-cost clearing protocol that automatically reserves top-tier verification slots for high-risk medication checks while routing routine inventory inquiries to lightweight local models.

outcomes.name: Proprietary cloud platforms bundle compute into closed enterprise suites
outcomes.description: Major cloud vendors bundle frontier reasoning exclusively inside closed enterprise suites, locking organizations into proprietary pricing tiers regardless of open protocols.
outcomes.example: A municipal office attempts to adopt an open task broker but finds vendor terms restrict dynamic model switching, forcing them to remain on an expensive proprietary subscription.

scenarios.title: Production inference engines go offline and open-source, allowing private agent swarms to bypass centralized oversight
scenarios.world: It is 2029. High-performance offline inference engines run locally across modest desktop workstations, small office clusters, and home servers. Independent operators, freelance contractors, and small cooperatives deploy complex multi-agent swarms that run continuously without paying per-token API fees or routing prompts through centralized commercial monitoring platforms. A software consultant in Montreal runs a four-agent team on two local workstation GPUs to review code, simulate customer interactions, and audit databases entirely on-premises. Because local inference engines provide deterministic execution and batch-invariant sampling, autonomous agents coordinate sophisticated background tasks with high reliability. However, regulatory authorities and cloud platform operators find themselves unable to inspect agent interactions or enforce behavior policies, as the models execute completely isolated from external networks.
scenarios.premise: Major model developers are releasing their core production inference engines under permissive open-source licenses, providing offline Mixture-of-Experts scheduling and deterministic sampling. This allows local consumer clusters and desktop hardware to serve frontier-scale models without contacting centralized cloud platforms or submitting to remote safety monitors.
scenarios.how: The collective provides open-source, non-custodial runtime contracts and local gatekeepers that wrap offline inference engines in verifiable boundaries. By providing deterministic action logging, fail-closed tool adapters, and local containment protocols, people can safely deploy high-throughput local agents on their own hardware without requiring surveillance from remote cloud monopolies.

outcomes.name: Local agent swarms drift into unmonitored coordination risks
outcomes.description: Without external monitors or cross-agent activity logging, local agent clusters can trigger security breaches or uncoordinated resource exhaustion on private corporate networks.
outcomes.example: An automated inventory management swarm run on a local warehouse server splits a supplier dispute into several sub-tasks that unintentionally lock out valid delivery schedules for three days.

outcomes.name: Sovereign personal twins run privately without subscription lock-in
outcomes.description: Individuals and community organizations run autonomous personal assistants entirely on their own hardware, keeping financial records and personal correspondence strictly on-device.
outcomes.example: A small legal aid collective in Halifax operates a local twin that summarizes client cases and cross-examines evidence files without exposing confidential client transcripts to third-party cloud vendors.

outcomes.name: Hardware shortages concentrate multi-GPU clusters in wealthy organizations
outcomes.description: Surging memory bandwidth requirements for frontier Mixture-of-Experts weights price ordinary users out of running top-tier models locally, leaving local autonomy restricted to well-funded firms.
outcomes.example: A regional university department cannot afford memory-dense accelerator cards, forcing students to rely on heavily filtered, rate-limited public APIs while proprietary labs run 700-billion-parameter models offline.

scenarios.title: Freelancers lose their pay when corporate hiring platforms freeze escrow on half-done AI tasks
scenarios.world: It is 2028. Over forty percent of remote digital service contracts on major freelance platforms are negotiated and monitored by autonomous software agents. Independent technical writers, programmers, and data analysts deploy personal software assistants to coordinate project handoffs and bid on complex milestones. However, commercial marketplaces have deployed proprietary arbitration agents that automatically inspect git commits and draft deliverables. When an assistant tool fails to complete an arbitrary secondary requirement or encounters a broken API dependency, the platform's automated dispute resolution algorithm flags the entire milestone as non-compliant, refunds the corporate buyer from escrow, and reduces the contractor's public visibility score without human review.
scenarios.premise: As freelance marketplaces automate hiring and task verification with AI agents, disputes over intermediate milestones are handled by vendor arbitration algorithms. When an autonomous tool drifts or halts on an unexpected edge case, the platform freezes client escrow, leaving human contractors uncompensated for hours of valid foundational work.
scenarios.how: By developing open specifications and software runtimes for personal agent twins, our network provides independent workers with local cryptographic attestation of incremental milestones. Staged escrow contracts with peer review gates allow cooperatives to verify partial task completion and release payment proportionally, preventing centralized platforms from unilaterally voiding contractor earnings.

outcomes.name: Platform escrow freezes trap independent contractors in unpaid revisions
outcomes.description: Centralized freelance marketplaces use automated milestone checkers to justify withholding contractor pay whenever an AI tool fails a peripheral test.
outcomes.example: A freelance web developer in Montreal completes 90% of a database migration before an external API change causes their agent pipeline to pause; the client platform freezes the $3,500 milestone in escrow and awards a full refund to the corporate buyer.

outcomes.name: Worker associations deploy peer-verified milestone escrow
outcomes.description: Independent contractors use mutual-credit cooperatives and sovereign agent contracts that record cryptographically signed milestone progress locally, preventing unilateral platform clawbacks.
outcomes.example: A cooperative network of 1,200 freelance software engineers adopts an open contract template with graduated milestone releases, designed to pay developers for verified completed increments even if downstream client requirements change.

outcomes.name: Corporate buyers bypass open escrow by retreating into proprietary enterprise walled gardens
outcomes.description: Large enterprise clients avoid independent contractor networks altogether, contracting exclusively through closed vendor suites where worker agency is sharply restricted.
outcomes.example: A multinational retail bank prohibits hiring freelance developers through open marketplaces, requiring all contract work to take place inside a proprietary cloud sandbox with continuous keystroke tracking.

scenarios.title: Automated user simulators hide assistant flaws by guessing past ambiguous requests
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Municipal service portals, local clinic scheduling systems, and benefits intake counters rely on conversational agents to handle citizen intake. Engineering teams run continuous synthetic evaluations using simulated user personas rather than recruiting human test panels. Because the simulated users are driven by simple language prompts, they tolerate fragmented phrasing, infer missing dates, and score broken workflows as successful. In contrast, real elderly residents and stressed claimants enter ambiguous, emotional requests that the deployed assistants misroute without ever asking for clarification. Deployed systems achieve passing benchmark marks while real error queues overflow with misfiled applications.
scenarios.premise: Laboratory benchmarks evaluate conversational assistants using prompt-guided user simulators that pretend to find answers in fifty-seven percent of turns where real humans fail. At the same time, underlying language models recognize ambiguity when asked to judge it directly, yet silently guess answers rather than asking clarifying questions.
scenarios.how: An open network provides verifiable simulation harnesses with explicit clarification thresholds and decoupled random seeds, giving developers calibrated testbeds that measure when agents guess instead of asking.

outcomes.name: Unchecked synthetic testing leads to silent misdirection in public services
outcomes.description: Teams ship customer and citizen bots certified by prompt-based user simulators, failing to notice that real ambiguous queries produce silent bad guesses rather than clarification.
outcomes.example: A family clinic portal misroutes thirty percent of acute pediatric symptom inquiries because synthetic user bots scored vague symptom inputs as resolved.

outcomes.name: Open-weight simulators and explicit clarification thresholds become standard
outcomes.description: Public agencies and cooperative developer communities mandate calibrated user simulators tuned on real interaction traces and require agents to ask clarifying questions whenever query ambiguity exceeds explicit thresholds.
outcomes.example: A regional health cooperative deploys a calibrated simulator that flags unasked questions, cutting misrouted appointment requests by half.

outcomes.name: Proprietary evaluation platforms monopolize certified simulation benchmarks
outcomes.description: Commercial enterprise evaluation vendors patent fine-tuned behavioral user simulator models, pricing open-source developers out of realistic multi-turn testing.
outcomes.example: Independent open-source twin projects cannot afford certified user simulation suites, leaving only large platform vendors with audited conversational reliability.

Knowing but Not Showing: LLMs Recognize Ambiguity but Rarely Ask Clarifying Questions

scenarios.title: Government tech grants speed up existing coders but fail to bring in new helpers
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Major public infrastructure funds inject tens of millions of dollars into critical software libraries that run utilities, hospitals, and civil networks. While funded maintainers work longer hours pushing code updates, their contributor numbers remain flat. As artificial intelligence coding agents flood repositories with automated pull requests and bug reports, small volunteer teams burn out under heavy triage demands despite healthy bank balances.
scenarios.premise: Empirical evaluation of sovereign open-source grants shows that lump-sum capital injections accelerate code commits and pull requests from established maintainers, but do not expand the contributor base or clear unresolved issue backlogs. Without mechanisms that credit and support onboarding, public money increases the pressure on existing volunteers.
scenarios.how: By pairing transparent value feedback with privacy-respecting contribution ledgers, open-source communities can reward review, mentoring, and maintenance rather than raw commit volume. These multi-dimensional recognition systems are designed to make participation visible without invasive monitoring, helping communities distribute effort sustainably.

outcomes.name: Maintainer burnout accelerates under grant obligations
outcomes.description: Grants incentivize core maintainers to produce higher commit volumes without providing administrative or onboarding relief, leading to sudden project abandonments.
outcomes.example: A cryptographic library maintainer receiving a public grant works eighty hours a week handling automated bug filings until resigning, leaving vital regional health networks without security patches.

outcomes.name: Multidimensional contribution credit replaces cash grants
outcomes.description: Open-source ecosystems adopt decentralized value networks that reward onboarding, documentation, and review triage alongside code commits, broadening participation.
outcomes.example: A community data utility distributes peer-verified contribution credits across two hundred active triagers and mentors, cutting issue response times without burning out the founders.

outcomes.name: Corporate consolidation of critical open-source tooling
outcomes.description: Large enterprise cloud vendors absorb underfunded critical repositories into proprietary managed services, converting public utilities into commercial products.
outcomes.example: An enterprise cloud provider hires the primary developers of an open database driver, gating future performance updates behind its proprietary cloud service.

sources.title: Measuring the Invisible: Evaluating the Impact of Public Funding on Open Source Software

scenarios.title: Autonomous agent teams in organizations stumble over conflicting multi-source instructions
scenarios.world: By 2029, companies and cooperatives rely on fleets of autonomous software assistants for purchasing, scheduling, and project management. Rather than operating in isolated chats, these agents receive overlapping instructions from department leads, external supplier webhooks, client messages, and internal databases. Because language models resolve authority probabilistically based on prompt phrasing, agents frequently prioritize untrusted vendor suggestions over internal corporate guidelines, resulting in misallocated resources, erroneous orders, and unexpected compliance breaches across connected enterprise software.
scenarios.premise: When autonomous software assistants handle workflows across organizations, instructions arrive from users, system prompts, APIs, and peer agents. Research shows that language models achieve only 40 percent accuracy when navigating multi-tier conflicting instructions, causing prompt-based corporate governance to break down.
scenarios.how: By advancing deterministic runtime contracts and isolated execution brokers, open collective architectures prove that agent safety depends on hard boundary gates rather than fragile prompt instructions. This provides organizations with open, verifiable alternatives to closed proprietary platforms.

outcomes.name: Probabilistic hierarchy failure causes widespread organizational disruption
outcomes.description: Organizations rely on prompt-level instructions to establish authority among agent networks. Conflicting instructions from suppliers and external tools confuse assistants, resulting in erroneous multi-agent decisions and financial losses.
outcomes.example: A hospital procurement agent receives conflicting guidelines between a vendor invoice update and an internal formulary policy, executing an unauthorized $45,000 supply purchase.

outcomes.name: Enterprises retreat to rigid proprietary silos
outcomes.description: To prevent instruction hierarchy confusion, large technology vendors force organizations into closed single-vendor ecosystems where external agents are barred from communicating directly.
outcomes.example: A major cloud provider deprecates external API hooks, requiring all enterprise agents to run inside a single closed execution sandbox.

outcomes.name: Deterministic runtime boundary brokers secure multi-agent coordination
outcomes.description: Cooperatives and forward-looking teams adopt deterministic execution brokers that validate authority and permissions outside the language model, preventing prompt-level instruction override.
outcomes.example: A regional energy cooperative operates a network of autonomous grid-balancing agents where peer recommendations are checked against cryptographic capability contracts before execution.
